py.u01.title: Open the story
py.u01.description: Give your adventure a setting and a surprise.
py.u01.learnTitle: Your story starts with one instruction
py.u01.learn: A program is a set of instructions. Python follows these instructions from top to bottom. Use print() to display words on the screen.
py.u01.detail: Put text inside matching quotation marks, then put that string inside the parentheses. Use lowercase print. The quotation marks do not appear in the output.
py.u01.example:
print("You arrive at a moonlit castle.")
print("A tiny dragon opens the gate.")
py.u01.exampleOutput:
You arrive at a moonlit castle.
A tiny dragon opens the gate.
py.u01.exampleNote: Each print() adds a new line. Two instructions give you two lines of story.
py.u01.question: Which message appears first?
py.u01.why: Python runs the first print statement before the second. Swapping the code lines swaps the messages.
py.u01.guided: Change the dragon into a different creature. Keep the matching quotes and parentheses, then run your story.
py.u01.starter:
# Describe a location with print()
# On the next line, print an unexpected event
py.u01.challenge: Write two print statements with two different story messages: first a place, then a surprise. The check makes sure you print two different messages that use words; whether they make a good scene is up to you.
hints: You need two print() lines: the first describes a place, the second something unexpected.
Check each line: lowercase print, then parentheses, with your message inside matching quotes.
A pattern to complete: print("You wake up in ___.") Then add a second print() with your surprise.

errorHints.text: Every opening quote needs a closing quote, and every ( needs a ). Check the end of each line.
print is all lowercase, and words need quotes around them. Without quotes, Python reads words as names.
Each message needs words, like the name of a place or something that happens.
Keep your first line as it is, and make the second one about something else that happens.

similarExample.note: One print() shows one line of text. Your challenge uses two, with your own words.

py.u01.title: Create your hero
py.u01.description: Give the adventure a hero and a useful tool.
py.u01.learnTitle: Remember a detail with a variable
py.u01.learn: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Write hero = "Nova" to store a name. Later, use hero without quotes to read the value.
py.u01.detail: The equals sign assigns a value; it does not print anything. print("hero") displays the word hero. print(hero) displays the value stored under that name. Define a variable before you use it.
py.u01.exampleNote: Changing the two assignments updates the character details without changing the print instructions.
py.u01.question: What does print(hero) display after hero = "Nova"?
py.u01.why: Without quotes, hero means “use the value stored in this variable.” That value is the string Nova.
py.u01.guided: Change Nova to your hero’s name and lantern to a tool of your choice. Run the code to see both values.
py.u01.starter:
hero = ""
tool = ""
# Print hero and tool, using the variables
py.u01.challenge: Store a nonempty hero name in hero and a nonempty tool in tool. Print both values by using the variables. You may add labels or combine them into a sentence.
hints: This card needs two variables, hero and tool, each holding some text. Then print() shows them.
Look at the first two lines: put your own words between the empty quotes. Then check your print(): a variable name goes inside it with no quotes.
With other names: pet = "___" stores text, and print(pet) shows it. Do the same with hero and tool.

errorHints.text: Names must be spelled exactly the same each time: hero in print() must match hero where you gave it a value, letter for letter.
Text values need matching quotes, like "Kai". Variable names inside print() do not.
If your output shows the words hero and tool instead of your values, remove the quotes around the names inside print().

similarExample.code:
pet = "Biscuit"
bed = "rug"
print(pet + " sleeps on the " + bed)
similarExample.note: Two variables hold text, and print() shows their values by name. Your challenge does the same with hero and tool.

otherWays.note: An f-string puts the values straight into the sentence.
print() can take several values separated by commas, and puts a space between them.

py.u01.title: Meet the player
py.u01.description: Let someone else name the hero.
py.u01.learn: input("What is your name? ") displays a prompt and returns the text the player types. Store that returned text in a variable so your story can use it.
py.u01.detail: Here, player = input(...) saves the response. A plus sign joins strings: "Welcome, " + player. In this academy, fill in Player replies before running; Python reads those replies in order.
py.u01.example:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome, " + player + "!")
py.u01.exampleNote: With Nova as the player reply, the welcome includes Nova. Try a different reply and the story changes.
py.u01.question: If the player replies Kai, what will the example display?
py.u01.why: input() returns Kai. The variable player remembers that text, and print() joins it to the greeting.
py.u01.guided: Change the welcome message. Run once with Nova as the reply, then change the reply to Kai and run again.
py.u01.starter:
player = input("What is your name? ")
# Print a welcome that uses player
py.u01.challenge: Ask for the player’s name with input(), store the reply, and print a greeting that includes that reply. It should work for different names without editing the code.
hints: input() gives back whatever the player typed. The starter already keeps it in the variable player.
Look at the comment line: replace it with a print() that joins a greeting and player.
With other names: print("Good morning, " + friend) greets whatever is stored in friend. An f-string works too: f"See you soon, {friend}".

errorHints.text: The reply is stored in player. Check that the name inside your print() is spelled exactly the same.
A name typed straight into the greeting stays the same for every player. Use the variable player in the greeting instead.

similarExample.note: A variable inside a greeting. In your challenge, the value comes from input() instead of being typed into the code.

otherWays.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Welcome, {player}!")
otherWays.note: An f-string puts the reply straight into the greeting.

otherWays.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome,", player)
otherWays.note: print() with a comma adds the space for you.

py.u01.title: Choose a path
py.u01.description: Make the story respond to a choice.
py.u01.learnTitle: Give your story two possible paths
py.u01.learn: An if statement runs an indented block only when its condition is true. == compares two values. An else block runs when that condition is false.
py.u01.detail: Use a colon after the if condition and after else. Indent the instructions inside each block by four spaces. Our example compares exact lowercase text: left. Any other reply takes the else path.
py.u01.exampleNote: With left as the reply, only the waterfall line runs. With right, only the library line runs.
py.u01.question: Which block runs when path is "right"?
py.u01.why: "right" == "left" is false, so Python skips the if block and runs the else block.
py.u01.guided: Give both paths new discoveries. Run with left, then with right. Confirm that the discoveries differ.
py.u01.starter:
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    # Print one discovery
    pass
else:
    # Print a different discovery
    pass
py.u01.challenge: Ask the player to choose left or right. Use if and else to print a different nonempty discovery for each choice. Keep the replies as lowercase left and right; invent your own discoveries.
hints: You need two branches: one when the reply is left, and one for anything else.
Look at the two pass lines in the starter. Each one is the place for a print() with a discovery.
A pattern from another story: if answer == "yes": then an indented print(...), then else: and another indented print(...).

errorHints.text: Lines inside if and else start with four spaces. Press Tab at the start of the line to add them.
The if and else lines end with a colon, and comparing uses two equals signs: ==.
Your two branches print the same thing. Change the words in one of them.

similarExample.note: One reply, two branches, a different message in each. Your challenge compares the reply with "left".

otherWays.note: != means "is not equal to", so the branches can be written the other way round.

py.u01.title: Launch your adventure
py.u01.description: Bring a player, a setting, and a choice into one small game.
py.u01.learnTitle: Connect the pieces into a game
py.u01.learn: You now know how to display a scene, store a value, ask for input, and choose a path. Combine them in order: set the scene, ask for a name, ask for a direction, then reveal an ending.
py.u01.detail: Keep each input response in its own variable. Use the player’s name in a printed message. Then use if/else to give left and right different endings. Test both paths before sharing your game.
py.u01.example:
print("A floating island appears.")
hero = input("Your name? ")
print("Welcome aboard, " + hero)
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    print("You befriend a cloud dragon.")
else:
    print("You discover a sky garden.")
py.u01.exampleOutput:
A floating island appears.
Welcome aboard, Nova
You befriend a cloud dragon.
py.u01.exampleNote: The same code welcomes different players and produces two endings. That is your first interactive adventure.
py.u01.question: What should you test before sharing the adventure?
py.u01.why: Different replies exercise different behavior. Testing names and both paths catches mistakes a single run might miss.
py.u01.guided: Remix the floating island into your own world. Change both endings and try different player replies.
py.u01.starter:
# Print your opening scene
hero = input("Your name? ")
# Welcome your hero by name
path = input("Left or right? ")
# Use if/else for two different endings
py.u01.challenge: Build your own adventure. Print an opening scene, ask for a name and welcome that player, then ask for left or right and use if/else for different endings. Your story words are up to you.
hints: Four parts, in order: an opening scene, a welcome that uses the name, the path question, and two different endings.
Each comment in the starter marks where a print() or the if/else goes. Fill them in from top to bottom.
Patterns from earlier lessons: print("Welcome, " + name) for the welcome, and if answer == "yes": then else: for the two endings.

errorHints.text: The player's name is stored in hero, and the path in path. Use those exact names.
Lines inside if and else start with four spaces.
Your very first line must be a print() with a scene, before the line that asks for a name.
Keep both input() lines from the starter: the name first, then the path.

similarExample.code:
print("The train doors open.")
rider = input("Ticket name? ")
print("All aboard, " + rider)
similarExample.note: A scene, a question and a welcome. Your adventure adds the path question and two different endings.

otherWays.code:
print("A storm rolls in.")
hero = input("Your name? ")
print(f"Welcome aboard, {hero}!")
path = input("Left or right? ")
if path == "left":
    print("You ride the lightning.")
else:
    print("You shelter in a lighthouse.")

fixture.u01.title: Add two numbers
fixture.u01.example:
a = int(input("First? "))
b = int(input("Second? "))
print(a * b)
fixture.u01.question: Which is a test?
fixture.u01.guided: Change one thing and run it.
fixture.u01.challenge: Ask for two whole numbers with input() and print their sum.
hints: You need two numbers from input(), turned into whole numbers, and then their sum.
Look at the line after the starter: ask for the second number the same way.
With other names: total = x + y adds two numbers, then print(total) shows it.

errorHints.text: Check that every name you print was given a value first, spelled the same way.
A negative number is still a number: adding -4 takes 4 away. Check that you add the two replies as they are.

similarExample.note: Two numbers and an operator. Your challenge reads its numbers with input() and adds them.

otherWays.code:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
total = a + b
print(total)
otherWays.note: Store the sum in a variable first.

fixture.u02.title: Double a number
fixture.u02.question: Which is a test?
fixture.u02.guided: Change one thing and run it.
fixture.u02.challenge: Ask for a whole number and print twice its value.
hints: Read one number, then print it multiplied by two.
Look at the line after the starter: print something with n in it.
With other names: print(x * 3) shows three times x.
